messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eleanor had always taken great pride in her role as a caregiver to her husband and family. So when her granddaughter passed away suddenly at a young age, Eleanor was consumed by an overwhelming sense of responsibility - she felt that she should have been able to protect the child, that somehow it was all her fault. As the days went by, this feeling of failed protection only intensified, leaving her with a deep sense of isolation and disconnection from others. As she struggled to come to terms with her loss, Eleanor found herself withdrawing from social interactions - avoiding gatherings with friends and family, even stopping attendance at her weekly book club. She told herself it was because she didn't want to burden others with her grief, but in truth, she felt like an outsider, someone who no longer belonged anywhere. This sense of isolation only reinforced her feeling that she had failed to protect those around her. As the months passed, Eleanor became increasingly consumed by a constant sense of tension - her body always on alert, ready to react to some unknown danger lurking just out of sight. Even in the safety of her own home, surrounded by loved ones, she couldn't shake off the feeling that something was about to go terribly wrong. She would try to distract herself with household chores or gardening, but even these tasks seemed to take on a sense of urgency - as if every moment not spent preparing for some unknown threat was a moment wasted. Her constant busyness became a way of coping with this perpetual state of hypervigilance - she would exhaust herself with work and activities just so that she could momentarily forget about the fear that gripped her. But no matter how hard she worked, the tension never fully dissipated, always lurking just beneath the surface. This constant feeling of being on edge only reinforced her negative emotions - anger, guilt, shame all swirling together in a toxic stew that seemed to have no end. Eleanor's feelings of isolation and failure also fed back into this cycle of threat - as she became increasingly withdrawn, she began to see danger lurking everywhere. Simple interactions with strangers became fraught with peril, every phone call or knock on the door a potential source of trauma. Her negative appraisals had created a self-fulfilling prophecy - by withdrawing from others and the world around her, Eleanor was indeed setting herself apart, reinforcing her own sense of isolation. One day, as she was struggling to get out of bed, exhausted from yet another sleepless night, Eleanor realized that something had to change. She couldn't keep living like this - constantly on edge, constantly afraid. With a newfound determination, she began reaching out for help, seeking support groups and therapy in the hopes of finally finding some peace. As she sat in her first session with a therapist, Eleanor felt a sense of trepidation wash over her. Would they be able to understand her pain? Would they be able to help her heal? The fear that had gripped her for so long still lingered, but for the first time in months, Eleanor felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, she could learn to let go of this crushing weight and find her way back to a life worth living.
